title: Linkability of GPS coordinates to child identity
description: Live GPS coordinates transmitted from child's device could be linked to the child's identity through device identifiers, timestamps, or other metadata, enabling tracking of the child's movements and activities.
assumptions: Backend stores or logs GPS data with identifying information; child's device has unique identifiers
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is a general linkability node; specific LINDDUN Pro node may vary

title: Identifiability through location data
description: GPS coordinates can reveal sensitive personal information about the child's home, school, workplace, and frequent locations, making the child identifiable even without explicit identifiers.
assumptions: Location patterns are consistent and identifiable; backend retains historical location data
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a general identifiability node; specific LINDDUN Pro node may vary

title: Unauthorized disclosure of location data
description: Live GPS coordinates could be disclosed to unauthorized parties through data breaches, insider threats, or improper access controls on the backend system.
assumptions: Backend has access controls; GPS data is stored or transmitted to third parties
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a general disclosure node; specific LINDDUN Pro node may vary

title: Excessive data collection via continuous GPS tracking
description: Continuous live GPS tracking may collect more location data than necessary for the stated purpose, violating data minimization principles.
assumptions: Purpose of GPS tracking is not clearly defined; continuous tracking may exceed what's needed
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is a general data minimization node; specific LINDDUN Pro node may vary

title: Usurpation of child's device for false location reporting
description: An unauthorized person could access the child's device and transmit false GPS coordinates, potentially misleading the backend about the child's actual location.
assumptions: Child's device is accessible to others; backend trusts GPS data without verification
uncertainty_note: Tree node U.1.1 is a general usurpation node; specific LINDDUN Pro node may vary

title: Unnecessary Location Data Storage
description: Backend writes each location ping to Location History Store, potentially storing more location data than strictly required for the service's core functionality. This violates the minimality principle - location data should only be retained as long as necessary and only when explicitly required.
assumptions: Location data is personal data that can identify individuals' movements and patterns
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] about data disclosure; the exact tree node may vary in LINDDUN Pro

title: Location History Linkability
description: Stored location history can be linked across time periods to create detailed movement profiles, potentially revealing sensitive patterns about user behavior, routines, and associations.
assumptions: Location data points can be correlated over time to build comprehensive user profiles
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is standard for linkability threats; based on general LINDDUN methodology

title: Location Data Identifiability
description: Location history data can be used to identify individuals, especially when combined with other data sources. Frequent or unique location patterns can serve as identifying characteristics.
assumptions: Location data can be correlated with other information to identify specific individuals
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is standard for identifiability threats; based on general LINDDUN methodology

title: Unnecessary Location Data Transfer to Geofencing Engine
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) forwards location pings to the Geofencing Engine (P2). This represents an explicit data disclosure where personal location data is transferred across a process boundary. The threat arises if the geofencing engine receives more location data than strictly necessary for zone entry/exit detection, violating the minimality principle.
assumptions: Location data is considered personal data; the geofencing engine may have access to more data than needed for its function.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] about data disclosure; the exact tree node may vary in LINDDUN Pro.

title: Location Data Linking Risk During Transfer
description: Location pings transferred from P1 to P2 could be linked with other data sources to create a comprehensive profile of user movements. The transfer creates a potential linking vector where the geofencing engine could correlate location data with other user information.
assumptions: The geofencing engine or downstream systems may have access to additional user data that could be linked with location information.
uncertainty_note: L.1.1 is a standard linking node; confidence based on general LINDDUN methodology.

title: Location Data Identification Risk
description: Location pings transferred to the Geofencing Engine could be used to identify individuals, especially when combined with timestamps and device identifiers. Even without explicit identifiers, precise location data can be identifying in certain contexts.
assumptions: Location data combined with timing information can be used to identify or track specific users.
uncertainty_note: I.1.1 is a standard identification node; confidence based on general LINDDUN methodology.

title: Identification of Family Members from Zone Definitions
description: Zone definitions (home, school, friend's house) stored in DS2 can reveal sensitive location information about family members, potentially enabling identification of individuals' daily routines and whereabouts.
assumptions: Zone definitions are stored with sufficient detail to infer individual locations
uncertainty_note: Using tree node I.1.1 based on context mapping for DataStore->Process flows

title: Linkability of Zone Data to Other Family Data
description: Zone definitions in DS2 can be linked with other family account data (e.g., contact info, schedules) to create comprehensive profiles of family members' movements and associations.
assumptions: Other data flows exist that could be correlated with zone definitions
uncertainty_note: Using tree node L.1.1 based on context mapping for DataStore->Process flows

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Zone Definitions
description: Geofencing Engine (P2) may expose zone definitions to unauthorized parties through improper access controls, logging, or data transmission during geofencing operations.
assumptions: P2 has access to zone definitions and may transmit or log them
uncertainty_note: Using tree node D.1.1 based on context mapping for DataStore->Process flows

title: Linkability of Geofencing Notifications
description: The arrival/departure notifications could be linked across multiple events to reconstruct the child's movement patterns and location history, potentially revealing sensitive behavioral information about when and where the child enters/exits defined zones.
assumptions: Notifications are transmitted in a way that allows correlation across time and zones
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 based on Process->ExternalEntity mapping context

title: Identification of Child's Location
description: The notifications directly identify the child's presence in specific geofenced zones, potentially revealing sensitive location information to unauthorized recipients or through data aggregation.
assumptions: Notifications contain or can be correlated with child identity information
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 based on Process->ExternalEntity mapping context

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Geofencing Data
description: The geofencing notifications could be disclosed to unauthorized parties (e.g., through interception, logging, or improper access), revealing the child's location patterns to entities without legitimate need-to-know.
assumptions: Notifications are transmitted over networks or stored in systems with inadequate access controls
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 based on Process->ExternalEntity mapping context

title: Usurpation of Notification Authority
description: An attacker could impersonate the Geofencing Engine to send false arrival/departure notifications, potentially misleading parents or guardians about the child's actual location and status.
assumptions: The notification system lacks proper authentication and integrity verification
uncertainty_note: Using U.1.1 based on Process->ExternalEntity mapping context

title: Parent-Child Identity Linkability
description: The parent's identity can be linked to the child's profile data (name, DOB, school) and geofence zones, potentially enabling tracking of the child's activities through the parent's account.
assumptions: Parent account is used to create and manage child profile

title: Child Identification via Profile Data
description: Child's personally identifiable information (name, DOB, school) in the profile can be used to identify the child, potentially exposing them to privacy risks.
assumptions: Child profile contains PII that can be used for identification

title: Child Profile Data Disclosure
description: Child's sensitive information (name, DOB, school) and geofence zones could be disclosed to unauthorized parties through the registration flow.
assumptions: Data transmitted from EE1 to P1 may be intercepted or accessed by unauthorized entities

title: Parent Identity Usurpation
description: An unauthorized actor could usurp the parent's identity to create a child profile, potentially misrepresenting the child's information or accessing geofence zones.
assumptions: Parent identity verification during registration may be insufficient

title: Child Privacy Regulation Non-Compliance
description: The registration flow may fail to comply with child privacy regulations (e.g., COPPA, GDPR-K) regarding collection and processing of children's personal data.
assumptions: System may not implement adequate consent mechanisms or data minimization for child data

title: Explicit Data Disclosure to DataStore
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) stores personal data including child profiles and geofence zone data in the Family Account & Permissions Store (DS2). This represents an explicit disclosure of personal data that must be justified under the minimality principle - only data strictly required should be stored.
assumptions: The backend is designed to store this data as part of its normal operation
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is inferred from context about explicit disclosures; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version

title: Identifiability of Stored Child Profile Data
description: Child profile data stored in DS2 contains personally identifiable information that could identify specific children. The data may be linked to parent accounts, creating additional identifiability risks.
assumptions: Child profile data includes names, ages, or other identifiers
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is inferred; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version

title: Data Integrity Risk for Geofence Zone Data
description: Geofence zone data stored in DS2 could be tampered with, leading to incorrect location-based access controls or safety features. Integrity violations could compromise child safety mechanisms.
assumptions: Geofence data is used for safety or access control purposes
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is inferred; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version

title: Linkability of Stored Account Data
description: Data stored in DS2 (account, child profile, geofence zones) could be linked across different data sources or time periods, potentially revealing patterns about family behavior, location history, or usage patterns.
assumptions: DS2 may be queried or accessed in conjunction with other data sources
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is inferred; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version

title: Linkability of Parent Identity to Location Data
description: An observer can link the parent's identity (EE1) to the child's location data being requested, potentially enabling tracking of the parent's access patterns to location information.
assumptions: Parent identity is transmitted or associated with the location request

title: Identification of Child's Location
description: The location data (current or historical) can be used to identify the child's whereabouts, movements, and routines, potentially revealing sensitive personal information about the child.
assumptions: Location data is precise enough to identify specific locations or patterns

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Location Data
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) may disclose the child's location data to unauthorized parties, including third-party services, advertisers, or malicious actors without proper consent.
assumptions: Location data is transmitted or stored in ways that expose it to unauthorized access

title: Manipulation of Location Data
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) could potentially alter, falsify, or manipulate the location data before it reaches the parent, leading to incorrect or misleading location information.
assumptions: P1 has the capability to modify location data in transit or at rest

title: Usurpation of Parent's Access Rights
description: An unauthorized actor could impersonate the parent (EE1) to gain access to the child's location data through the Mobile App Backend (P1), potentially through credential theft or session hijacking.
assumptions: Authentication mechanisms are vulnerable to impersonation attacks

title: Non-compliance with Privacy Regulations
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) may fail to comply with privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, COPPA) regarding the collection, processing, and disclosure of children's location data.
assumptions: Location data of children is subject to stricter privacy regulations

title: Identification of child's location data
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) processes and stores the child's location data, which can be used to identify the child's movements, routines, and whereabouts. This identification risk is inherent in any system that tracks and stores location information.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of child's location to secondary guardian
description: The system may disclose the child's location data to the secondary guardian (e.g., grandparent) without proper authorization or consent verification. This could occur if the invitation mechanism lacks adequate access controls or if the guardian's identity is not properly verified.

title: Linkability of parent and child location data
description: The Mobile App Backend (P1) can link the parent's identity with the child's location data through the invitation process. This creates a privacy risk where the parent's association with the child's movements can be tracked and potentially misused.

title: Parent's disclosure of child's location to unauthorized parties
description: The parent (EE1) may inadvertently or intentionally share the child's location data with unauthorized third parties when inviting a secondary guardian. This could occur if the parent lacks awareness of privacy implications or if the invitation process lacks safeguards.

title: Impersonation of parent in invitation process
description: An attacker could potentially impersonate the parent (EE1) to the Mobile App Backend (P1) and initiate an invitation to a secondary guardian, thereby gaining unauthorized access to the child's location data.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Child's Live Location
description: The secondary guardian (EE3) may receive and potentially share the child's live location data with unauthorized third parties, violating the child's privacy expectations.
assumptions: Secondary guardian has access to the data and may share it further

title: Linkability of Location Data with Other Information
description: The secondary guardian could link the child's live location data with other available information to create a detailed profile of the child's movements and habits.
assumptions: Secondary guardian has access to additional data sources

title: Identification of Child from Location Patterns
description: The secondary guardian could identify the specific child being tracked through location patterns and context, even if the child's identity is not explicitly transmitted.
assumptions: Location data reveals identifiable patterns

title: Unauthorized Access to Location Data
description: Unauthorized parties could potentially intercept or access the child's live location data during transmission from the backend to the secondary guardian.
assumptions: Transmission channel may not be fully secured

title: Potential Regulatory Non-Compliance
description: Sharing a child's live location data with a secondary guardian may violate GDPR or other privacy regulations regarding children's data protection and consent requirements.
assumptions: Applicable privacy regulations require explicit consent for children's location data
uncertainty_note: Regulatory requirements vary by jurisdiction

title: Linkability of Aggregated Analytics Data
description: Even though data is described as 'aggregated', there is a risk that usage and engagement patterns could be linked with other datasets (e.g., device IDs, IP addresses, or other partner data) to re-identify individual users or create detailed user profiles.
assumptions: Partner may have access to additional data sources that could be combined with this analytics data
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 based on general LINDDUN methodology for linkability threats in Process→ExternalEntity flows

title: Unauthorized Disclosure to Third Parties
description: The advertising/analytics partner may share or sell the received analytics data to additional third parties beyond the original agreement, leading to unauthorized disclosure of user engagement information.
assumptions: Partner may have business incentives to monetize data beyond the stated purpose
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 for disclosure threats in Process→ExternalEntity flows

title: Excessive Data Collection and Sharing
description: The backend may share more detailed usage and engagement data than necessary for the advertising/analytics purpose, violating data minimization principles.
assumptions: Aggregated data may still contain identifiable patterns or metadata that exceeds what's needed for analytics
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 for data minimization threats in Process→ExternalEntity flows

title: Unintended Data Usage by Partner
description: The advertising/analytics partner may use the received analytics data for purposes beyond the agreed-upon funding of the app's free tier, such as building user profiles for targeted advertising or selling to data brokers.
assumptions: Partner may have broader business objectives that conflict with the stated data-sharing purpose
uncertainty_note: Using U.1.1 for usability/usage threats in Process→ExternalEntity flows

title: Child's location data can be identified
description: The manual check-in/SOS message contains the child's current location, which combined with the SOS context can directly identify the child's identity and whereabouts. This location data is personally identifiable information that could be used to track or locate the child.
assumptions: The location data is transmitted in a format that preserves identifiability

title: Child's location can be linked with other data
description: The child's location data from the SOS/check-in message could be linked with other data sources (e.g., other check-ins, device identifiers, parent information) to create a more complete profile of the child's movements and habits.
assumptions: Other data sources exist that could be correlated with this location data

title: Child's location data could be disclosed to unauthorized parties
description: The child's location information transmitted in the SOS/check-in message could be disclosed to unauthorized parties through system vulnerabilities, improper access controls, or data breaches, potentially exposing the child's whereabouts to malicious actors.
assumptions: The system has access controls that may not be fully effective

title: Child's location data could be used by unauthorized parties
description: Unauthorized parties who gain access to the child's location data could use it for stalking, harassment, or other harmful purposes, especially given the sensitive nature of SOS messages indicating potential emergencies.
assumptions: Unauthorized access to the system is possible
